structure.title: SE Intimation.pdf
structure.summary: Cipla Ltd. notifies BSE, NSE, and Luxembourg Stock Exchange of its 89th AGM on July 16, 2025, via video conferencing, enclosing the AGM Notice and Integrated Annual Report for FY 2024-25, with details on e-voting dates, eligibility, and website availability. Special business includes ratification of Cost Auditor remuneration for FY 2025-26 and appointment of Secretarial Auditors for five years.

nodes.title: NOTES:

nodes.title: TDS on Dividend Amount
nodes.summary: The text outlines TDS on dividends effective after April 1, 2020, detailing tax deduction rules for resident individuals (10% above ₹10,000 with valid PAN, nil with Forms 15G/15H under specified income limits, 20% for invalid PAN), other resident shareholders (10% without threshold or lower certificate, 20% for invalid PAN), and specific exempt entities (mutual funds, insurers, AIFs, government) requiring self-declarations and registration certificates. Non-resident shareholders face 20% plus surcharge/cess, with DTAA benefits available upon submitting PAN, TRC, Form 10F, and a self-declaration covering residency, beneficial ownership, and PE absence. Submission links and Rule 37BA declarations for assessee other than shareholder are also provided.

nodes.title: General Instructions:
nodes.summary: The text covers tax-related instructions for shareholders, including TDS rates and conditions for resident and non-resident shareholders, DTAA benefits, and the process for TDS certificates and Form 26AS. It outlines the shareholder's responsibility for tax demands arising from misrepresentation and advises seeking professional tax advice. Additionally, it provides details on the live webcast of the AGM, e-voting results declaration by the Chairman, and the publication of results on the Company and NSDL websites and communication to stock exchanges.

nodes.title: INSTRUCTIONS FOR MEMBERS FOR ATTENDING THE AGM THROUGH VC ARE AS UNDER:
nodes.summary: The text outlines instructions for members attending the AGM via video conferencing through the NSDL e-voting system. Members can join 15 minutes before and throughout the AGM, with technical support available via email or phone contacts. It advises using stable Wi-Fi/LAN to avoid audio/video issues. Members wishing to speak or ask questions must pre-register by July 15, 2025, providing name, DP ID, client ID/folio, PAN, and mobile number to a specified email. Only registered speakers may participate, and the company may limit speakers based on time.

nodes.title: Caring For Life
nodes.summary: Cipla’s 90-year journey from 1935 is driven by a mission to make healthcare accessible to all, prioritizing compassion over profit. The text highlights efforts in making India self-reliant in healthcare, supplying affordable drugs for HIV/AIDS and malaria, and supporting initiatives like the Cipla Palliative Care & Training Centre. It celebrates a legacy of compassion, care, innovation, and patient commitment, honoring Dr. Y K Hamied’s vision and scientific spirit, symbolized by his handwritten chemistry notes in the Annual Report. Cipla reaffirms its belief that healthcare is a right, not a privilege, and remains focused on patient needs and innovation, with the unchanged purpose: Caring for Life.

nodes.title: About this Report
nodes.summary: This text introduces Cipla's eighth Integrated Annual Report for FY 2024-25, covering financial and non-financial performance, including strategic initiatives, governance, environmental stewardship, and social responsibility. It outlines reporting guidelines based on the IIRC <IR> Framework, GRI Standards 2021, UN SDGs, and Indian regulations. The report presents the business model, strategies, governance, and performance across six capitals. It defines the reporting boundary (global operations, April 2024-March 2025) and scope (subsidiaries for non-financial reporting, entity list on page 325). It includes a Board responsibility statement, assurance details (statutory auditor for financials, DNV for non-financials), feedback contact information, and an overview of Cipla's history, global presence, product portfolio, and mission.

nodes.title: About Cipla 1
nodes.summary: Cipla, founded in 1935, is a global pharmaceutical company ranking third in India and second in South Africa's prescription market, among other rankings. It has 46 manufacturing sites producing over 50 dosage forms and 1,500 products for 74 markets. Its portfolio includes complex generics in respiratory, anti-retroviral, urology, cardiology, anti-infectives, and CNS areas, with R&D leveraging data science and digital technology. Key markets are India, South Africa, North America, and other regulated and emerging markets. Cipla's 2001 introduction of low-cost triple anti-retroviral therapy for HIV/AIDS in Africa is highlighted. The company emphasizes resource efficiency, medicine availability, financial performance, responsible business, sustainable growth, and its 'Caring for Life' mission. The text includes references and a website link.

nodes.title: Financial Highlights
nodes.summary: The text presents financial highlights including revenue from operations with a 10% five-year CAGR across FY 2019-20 to FY 2024-25, PAT and PAT margin with a 28% CAGR, EBITDA and EBITDA margin with a 17% CAGR, and RoIC trends. It notes FY 2024-25 revenue growth of 7% YoY, EBITDA margin of 25.9%, PAT margin of 19.1%, and ROIC growth of 208 BPS. Footnotes explain EBITDA, PAT, and RoIC calculations and one-time impacts. Additionally, it covers global reach with 42% revenue contribution and 7% YoY growth, detailing One-India business (branded prescription, trade generics, consumer health) with specific achievements, and North America business including market share, revenue, portfolio updates, approvals, and filings.

nodes.title: Global Reach 1
nodes.summary: The text covers Cipla's annual report for 2024-25, detailing performance across geographies. In India (42% revenue, 7% YoY growth), it highlights branded prescription (61.5% chronic share, 26 brands >₹100 Cr, Foracort >₹900 Cr), trade generics (7 brands >₹50 Cr, 19 launches, distribution expansion), and consumer health (top brands, illness-to-wellness focus, EBITDA margins). North America (29% revenue, 3% YoY growth) reported $934M revenue, 1.66% EUTRx share, respiratory and peptide growth, and approvals/filings. One Africa (14% revenue, 12% YoY growth) is second largest player, with private market growth 1.3x market, 18 launches, 77% private share. API (2% revenue, 5% YoY growth) shows emerging market growth. Emerging Markets and Europe (12% revenue, 15% YoY growth) include rankings in Sri Lanka/Nepal, lung leadership, and oncology/respiratory filings.

nodes.title: Chairman’s Message
nodes.summary: Chairman Y K Hamied reflects on Cipla's 90-year journey since its 1935 founding, emphasizing affordable medicine access, R&D and innovation with a humanitarian purpose of 'Caring for Life.' He highlights contributions in respiratory care, anti-retroviral HIV/AIDS drugs in Africa, and palliative care, and shares personal pride in his involvement. He underscores values like imagination and enthusiasm, acknowledges the 30,000-strong workforce, partners, medical community, management, board and shareholders, and thanks Mr M K Hamied for his visionary leadership. The document also briefly notes the MD & GCEO's message on quality, automation, digital quality systems and data integrity.

nodes.title: MD & GCEO’s Message 1
nodes.summary: Cipla's MD & GCEO message reflects on its 90-year journey of 'Caring for Life,' highlighting FY 2024-25 achievements: highest-ever EBITDA margin, 7% YoY growth in One India business crossing ₹11,000 crore, North America revenue of USD 934 million, 12% growth in One Africa, and 15% growth in EMEU. Quality remains a key pillar with automation, digital systems, and data integrity enhancements; regulatory inspections yielded VAI from USFDA and EU GMP compliance. Sustainability milestones include water positivity in India, 58% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 emissions, 64% renewable electricity, and Zero Waste to Landfill certification. Cipla ranked 3rd globally in pharma by S&P Global CSA. The Cipla Foundation advanced palliative care, cancer care, education, and community initiatives in India and South Africa. People-first culture earned 'Great Place To Work®' for the seventh consecutive year. Innovation focus includes respiratory (Lung Leadership), AMR, wellness, oncology, CNS, obesity, and partnerships in mRNA, biosimilars, and CAR-T therapy. The message concludes with a forward-looking commitment to growth, innovation, and patient-centric care.

nodes.title: Caring for Life Since 1935
nodes.summary: This text outlines Cipla's 90-year history since its 1935 founding by Dr. K A Hamied, driven by a mission of accessible healthcare and innovation. Key milestones include Mahatma Gandhi's 1939 visit inspiring self-sufficiency, Dr. Y K Hamied joining in 1960 and pioneering indigenous APIs, the 1972 launch of India's first inhaler, 1985 US FDA approvals, the 1997 establishment of a palliative care center, the 2001 offering of a low-cost HIV triple-drug combination, and 2013-2016 global acquisitions in South Africa and the USA. The narrative emphasizes humanitarian ethos and a legacy of building a healthier future.

nodes.title: Strategy for Strengthening Our Core Engines and Building Future Capabilities
nodes.summary: The text outlines a strategy for strengthening core engines and building future capabilities. It begins with the company's history since 1935, focusing on affordable, quality healthcare and patient-centricity over nine decades. It then describes the global healthcare landscape's rapid transformation driven by biosciences, AI, and technology, which has reduced drug costs and development time. It highlights advanced modalities like mRNA, CAR-T, gene therapy, ADCs, mAbs, and BsAbs that are setting new standards for better outcomes. The company commits to building deep capabilities and leveraging its execution engine to achieve Strategic Vision 2028.

nodes.title: Lung Leadership
nodes.summary: The text covers Cipla's strategies in three areas: Lung Leadership, Wellness, and New Therapy Frontiers. For Lung Leadership, it details dominance in India's respiratory market, digital tools like CipAir and Spirofy, a diversified pipeline beyond asthma/COPD, green propellant inhalers, global filings and launches, and Spirofy's expansion. In Wellness, it aims to be the largest consumer healthcare company in India and South Africa, with leading brands, acquisitions, and South Africa's OTC market growth. New Therapy Frontiers focuses on strengthening CNS, oncology, and obesity portfolios, including in-licensing Sanofi's CNS range and top rankings in South Africa and Morocco.

nodes.title: Cipla Annual Report: Wellness Growth and New Therapy Frontiers
key_items: New Therapy Frontiers : Central Nervous System ('CNS'), Oncology and Obesity
nodes.summary: The page covers Cipla's aim to become the largest consumer healthcare company in India and South Africa, detailing strategies like building top-ranked consumer brands, expanding into emerging segments (skin, hair, weight management, gut health), and leveraging consumer insights. It highlights six CHL brands ranked #1 or #2 in categories such as pain recovery and nicotine replacement, and FY 2024-25 acquisitions (e.g., Astaberry, Ikin) expanding distribution. In South Africa, the OTC market is valued at USD 1.1 billion, with Wellness revenues of ZAR 1.65 billion growing 11.8%, top 3 ranks in allergy and cold preparations, and integration of Actor Pharma. It also introduces new therapy frontiers in CNS, oncology, and obesity.

We in-licensed Sanofi’s India Central Nervous System ('CNS') product range including Frisium ®, a leading brand in anti-epileptic category, which has helped us gain our rank in CNS therapy to #5 position.
Currently, we hold the top-ranking positions in South Africa and Morocco markets in the CNS therapy area. To strengthen our position further, we will continue to focus on bringing in differentiated assets across the therapy in these countries.

nodes.title: Oncology
nodes.summary: The text outlines an oncology strategy focused on prevalent cancers in the Indian subcontinent through targeted therapies and supportive care. It cites global market growth from USD 255 billion in FY 2023-24 to over USD 400 billion by 2028, and WHO projections of 35 million new cancer cases by 2050, especially in low- and middle-income countries. The company highlights its history, from introducing Vincristine and Vinblastine in India in 1984 to developing nanotech products like paclitaxel injection. It notes successful launches, including Lenalidomide in the USA for multiple myeloma, mantle cell lymphoma, and myelodysplastic syndromes, and US FDA approval of Nilotinib capsules for chronic myeloid leukemia. Finally, it discusses advances in genomics driving precision and personalized medicine, and the company's ongoing exploration of new treatment platforms to bring advanced oncology solutions to LMICs.

nodes.summary: The text outlines a strategy to bring innovative assets to the world, focusing on building an innovation engine through in-house capabilities and strategic alliances. Efforts are classified into Horizon 2 (biosimilars, specialty, complex injectables, peptides, long-acting injectables) and Horizon 3 (advanced new-age technology). For Horizon 2, capabilities are being built for biosimilars, specialty peptides, long-acting injectables, and specialty products, including a new in-vitro discovery biology facility and a bio-assay lab with Kemwell Biopharma. For Horizon 3, new-age platforms like cell and gene therapy, mRNA, and stem cells are being developed for long-term competitive advantage, aiming to pioneer transformative stem cell therapies for unmet medical needs globally. Collaboration with investee company Ethris GmBH to co-develop mRNA assets for India and LMICs, and setting up an mRNA R&D laboratory and Centre of Excellence in Europe, are also covered.

This strongly complements our core business and also offers us a competitive edge in delivering solutions spanning across the entire healthcare continuum.

nodes.title: Breathefree
nodes.summary: The text introduces "Breathefree," a respiratory platform with over 1.5 million downloads that aids patients with asthma and COPD through action plans, exercises, reminders, content, and health tracking. A gamification module was launched to encourage adherence. The aim is to explore non-invasive digital screening for undiagnosed patients and provide a holistic platform from awareness to adherence. Building on FY 2023-24 vision, Breathefree Lung Wellness Centres (BLWCs) will open in Delhi and Mumbai, envisioned as centres of excellence in Diagnostics, Awareness, Research, and Training (DART). BLWCs will train clinicians and technicians and contribute to real-world research, reinforcing the purpose of "Caring for Life" by enabling access, innovation, and impact at the point of care.

nodes.title: Point of Care devices
nodes.summary:
Point of Care devices
We launched CipAir, an AI- powered mobile application, to simplify asthma screening in India with state-of- the-art proprietary technology that uses breathing signatures for Asthma screening. During FY 2025-26, we are planning to launch CipA1cDuo®, India’s unique handheld device that detects both HbA1c and Blood Glucose in a single prick of blood.
We have also developed CipOscillo® - Cipla’s Oscillometer in collaboration with a US-FDA approved technology partner. The license application has been filed with Indian regulators in FY 2024-25. CipOscillo® uses simple tidal breathing and is a portable battery operated oscillometer that detects airway obstruction within minutes and especially relevant for Paediatric and Geriatric patients.

nodes.title: One India
nodes.summary: One India aims for ₹20,000 crores revenue by FY 2027-28, touching 400 million lives through leadership in core therapies via best practices and innovation. Strategy includes new launches (inhaled insulin Afrezza, AMR, respiratory), building brands like Foracort and Omnigel, and celebrating 90 years in India. Growth was driven by large brands (Foracort, Dytor, etc.). Focus areas: multifold growth in chronic portfolio (Dytor, Humalog, Metolar) and obesity drugs; top five in diabetes, ophthalmology, dermatology; top three in cardiology. Foracort reached ₹900 crores, ranking No.1 for second year. IPM ranks: 2nd in Urology, 5th in CNS. Partnership with Orchid Pharma for AMR drug Cefepime+Enmetazobactam. Strengthened core business via regional/channel dominance, joint #1 in ₹300 crores brand club (six brands), launched 85 products, expanded field force from 10,470 to 11,512. Trade generics transitioned to new distribution model, expanded retail to over 1.5 lakh pharmacies, introduced new products, invested in digital capabilities, and expanded consumerisation initiatives.

nodes.title: One Africa
nodes.summary: The text outlines One Africa's aim to rank first in South Africa's private market, highlighting FY 2024-25 growth of 270 basis points above the market (6.7% vs 4.9%), being the only top-five player to organically grow the base business (0.03% vs -2.7%), ranking third with 8.6% market share and ZAR 5.1 billion revenue, and ranking second in Rx and third in OTC. It also covers strong performance in Ghana (nine times revenue growth and new launches), Kenya (leader in respiratory therapy, second in gastro-intestinal and pain), and the fully integrated North Africa business in Morocco and Algeria, with Morocco growing 150 basis points ahead of the total private market. The strategy emphasizes sharper focus on top cities, targeting the 'Missing Middle' segment, and growing North Africa while strengthening South African leadership.

nodes.title: North America
nodes.summary: North America achieved USD 918 million in FY 2024-25, marking 10 years of direct US market presence. Strategy focuses on deepening complex generics (LAI, peptides, 505b2), becoming the second largest generic inhalation player by 2030, and investing in selective biosimilars for respiratory and oncology. Albuterol MDI expansion led to the No. 1 generic inhalation position; ANDAs filed for gSymbicort and gQVAR, with manufacturing investments at Long Island and Fall River. Complex generics progress includes nanotech cancer products like paclitaxel injection, two launched peptide injections, three CGT-exclusive injections, and Nilotinib capsules approval (launch FY 2025-26). Future growth expects one complex oncology injection, four peptide injections, two respiratory products, plus investments in oligonucleotides and differentiated 505(b)2 products.

Governance is driven by a cloud-based BI dashboard for real-time QMS metrics and KPIs. A Digital Transformation Programme includes Gen AI use cases for complaint management, documentation review, and audit trail review. nodes.title: Double Materiality Assessment 1

The approach follows CSRD, ESRS 1, and EFRAG IG 1 guidelines. A contextual analysis shortlisted 17 material topics, with 10 prioritized based on stakeholder input. Impacts, Risks, and Opportunities (IROs) were reviewed with management, assessed for impact and financial materiality, and aligned with the ERM framework. Third-party assurance is mentioned. nodes.title: Pharmacovigilance

In FY 2024-25, 6,326 complaints were received and 5,489 resolved. Medical review precedes CIOMS/MedWatch reporting. GVP and signal detection with bi-annual Drug Safety Review Committee reviews are followed; no Indian product was listed in safety alerts. Digitisation and automation include Leucine 4.0 cleaning validation. The Corporate Sterility Assurance Program (2023) develops standards, KPIs, reviews, CCS documents for EU GMP. Internal audits and a robust QMS cover all Indian sites and the US Fall River facility, plus drug-device QMS and ISO 13485:2016 certification at Jay Precision. Quality risk management includes SOP simplification and effectiveness checks.

nodes.title: Data Integrity and Security

The Enterprise Privacy Management Policy aligns with global standards like EU GDPR, SA POPI, US CCAF, and India DPDPA. Acceptable Usage and Incident Management policies define conduct and corrective measures. Security standards include NIST, ISO 27001, OWASP, and Enterprise Digital Risk Management. Policies are accessible via intranet, and the Data Privacy Management Policy is available online. Contact points for privacy queries and grievances are provided. All incidents are investigated per internal protocols, with a 24/7 Security Operations Centre using an XDR platform. One attempted cybersecurity incident in FY 2024-25 caused no data loss or adverse impact. Three internal vulnerability assessments and two external penetration tests were conducted, supported by a vulnerability management platform.

nodes.title: Human Rights Training 26

nodes.title: Our Guiding Philosophy 1
nodes.summary: The text outlines Cipla's social initiatives under the Cipla Foundation, guided by 'Caring for Life,' focusing on health, environmental sustainability, education, skilling, and disaster response. It details governance through the Board, CSR Committee, and Cipla Foundation, and reports FY 2024-25 social expenditure and beneficiary reach. A major focus is enhancing community health, especially palliative care, through the Cipla Palliative Care and Training Centre, partnerships like CanSupport, policy advocacy (Goa's palliative care policy), and integration into public hospitals (Nair Hospital, AIIMS Jodhpur, South Goa District Hospital) and new government collaborations. It highlights expanded reach, training, and partnership meetings to strengthen the palliative care ecosystem.

nodes.title: Palliative Care beyond Cancer
nodes.summary: Cipla's palliative care beyond cancer covers chronic illnesses like heart disease, COPD, kidney disorders, and Alzheimer's. Initiatives include neuro-palliative care at NIMHANS, Bengaluru, training social workers and treating over 1,100 patients; Sukoon Nilaya, Mumbai, expanding beds from 18 to 24 and engaging municipal hospitals; collaboration with St. John's National Academy, Bengaluru, providing holistic care for neurological, cardiac, and renal disorders, training staff, and benefiting over 1,700 patients; and paediatric palliative care at BJ Wadia Hospital, Mumbai, strengthening home care and training professionals, plus the Paediatric Palliative Care Leadership Programme in Hyderabad with workshops and online sessions for cross-border collaboration.

nodes.title: Paediatric Palliative Care
nodes.summary: Cipla's FY 2024–25 report details new government collaborations for palliative care with AIIMS Bathinda, AIIMS Mangalgiri, Sion Hospital, TMC Mullanpur, and others. It covers palliative care beyond cancer for chronic illnesses, including neuro-palliative care at NIMHANS (1,100+ patients), Sukoon Nilaya expansion to 24 beds, and St. John’s holistic care (1,700+ patients). Paediatric palliative care includes BJ Wadia Hospital home care and a leadership programme. The Saath-Saath helpline network (30+ organizations, 27 cities) received 5,000+ calls and added an AI chatbot. Public system partnerships with SNEHA focus on maternal and child health (1,03,000+ pregnant women). Thalassemia support provided BMTs for 68 patients and 1,650+ transfusions for 145+ patients. Mobile Health Units delivered 1.07 lakh consultations. South Africa projects include CCMDD (272,473 patients), Miles for Smiles (63+ surgeries), and Ajuga early childhood development (878 learners).

nodes.title: Palliative Care Helpline, Public Partnerships, Maternal Health, Thalassemia and Mobile Healthcare

nodes.summary: The text covers Saath-Saath, a PAN India palliative care helpline launched in 2021, connecting patients to providers via a network of 30+ organizations across 27 cities, with a multilingual AI chatbot and over 5,000 calls. It details a Public System Partnership with SNEHA in Mumbai slums to promote health-seeking behavior, focusing on maternal and child health. It describes SNEHA's Maternal and Child Health Programme providing nine essential services and reaching over 103,000 pregnant women. It outlines support for thalassemia patients, including medication, transfusions, and bone marrow transplants for 68 patients and 145+ major patients with 1,650+ transfusions. Finally, it covers Mobile Healthcare Units operated by HelpAge India, providing 1.07 lakh consultations across 207 locations in four states.

Education initiatives include mobile science labs, scholarships, digital learning, and girl child education. Skilling programs empower low-income individuals and support pharmaceutical training. Disaster response includes flood relief in Bihar and Tamil Nadu and participation in the PM Internship Scheme.

Community engagement, monitoring, awareness campaigns, and Biodiversity Management Plans are highlighted for fostering stewardship. nodes.title: Cipla’s strong financial management system combines several financial functions, such as accounting, fixed-asset management, treasury, revenue recognition and payment processing.
nodes.summary: Cipla's financial management integrates accounting, fixed-asset management, treasury, revenue recognition, and payment processing for real-time visibility and day-to-day operations, creating stakeholder value. The document highlights FY 2024-25 financial performance: 7% YoY consolidated revenue growth to ₹27,548 crores, driven by One-India, North America, South Africa, Emerging Markets, and Europe; EBITDA of ₹7,128 crores with 25.9% margin; highest-ever PAT of ₹5,273 crores (28% YoY growth) with 19.1% margin; and 10% five-year revenue CAGR. It covers working capital management with cash conversion cycle trends, working capital turnover ratio, cash flow from operations, free cash flow, and a dividend of ₹16 per share including a special dividend of ₹3. Key metrics include ROIC, EBITDA margin expansion, and capital allocation strategy.

nodes.title: PAT Growth and Working Capital Optimisation at Cipla
key_items: Optimising working capital and cash conversion cycle
nodes.summary: The page highlights Cipla's record Profit After Tax (PAT) of ₹5,273 crores in FY 2024-25, a 28% YoY growth and 28% five-year CAGR, with PAT and PAT margin data from FY 2019-20 to FY 2024-25. It also covers working capital management, including the cash conversion cycle trends from FY 2019-20 to FY 2024-25 and working capital and turnover ratio figures for the same period. The company's efforts to optimise inventory, receivables, and payables, enhance liquidity, mitigate supply disruption risks, and ensure continuous product supply are described.

nodes.title: Cash flow from operations and free cash flow
nodes.summary: The text discusses cash flow from operations and free cash flow, highlighting record profits and an improved cash conversion cycle that enabled consistent cash generation. It announces a dividend per share of H 16 for FY 2024-25, including a special dividend of H3 per equity share for 90 years of excellence, reinforcing shareholder value commitment. It presents trends in cash flow from operations and free cash flow across fiscal years 2019-20 to 2024-25, with figures in crores. Definitions are provided for cash conversion cycle, working capital, and working capital turnover ratio.

nodes.title: Sustained value creation
nodes.summary: The text discusses sustained value creation through effective capital management, highlighting rising ROIC and EPS ratios and a stable ROE trend as indicators of Cipla's ability to generate shareholder returns, allocate capital efficiently, and sustain profitability. It includes numerical data for ROIC from FY 2019-20 to FY 2024-25 (ranging from 12.5% to 33.1%), ROE over the same period (10.1% to 18.2%), and diluted EPS (19.16 to 65.24), emphasizing Cipla's commitment to maximizing shareholder value and financial robustness.

nodes.title: Reduced net debt ratios
nodes.summary: The text highlights Cipla's reduced net debt ratios, emphasizing financial prudence through negative net debt to equity and net debt to EBITDA ratios, and an improving interest coverage ratio. It provides specific ratio values across fiscal years 2019-20 to 2024-25 for net debt to equity, net debt to EBITDA, and interest coverage. It also includes footnotes defining free cash flow, RoIC, RoE, and the calculation of total borrowings and net debt.

nodes.title: Other key financial highlights Employee expenses:
nodes.summary: The text highlights Cipla's FY 2024-25 financials: employee expenses rose 12% to ₹4,833 crores due to increments, performance-linked components, and field force expansion; other expenses increased 4.8% to ₹6,658 crores (24.2% of revenue); depreciation and amortization were ₹1,107 crores; finance cost decreased to ₹62 crores; effective tax rate was 22.4% due to reversal of tax provisions. Leverage improved with debt-to-equity at 0.01 and net cash positive. Operating profit margin was 21.9%. Key ratios include debtors' turnover 5.4, return on net worth 18.2%, inventory turnover 1.6, current ratio 4.2, debt-service coverage 47.83, operating profit ratio 21.9%, and net profit margin 19.1%. No material changes occurred post-year-end. R&D expenditure was ₹1,536 crores (5.6% of revenue), with a chart showing historical R&D spend and intensity, and progress on priority assets.

nodes.title: Abbreviated New Drug Application ("ANDA") and New Drug Application ("NDA") portfolio and pipeline
nodes.summary: The text covers Cipla's ANDA/NDA portfolio reference, capital allocation policy balancing cash retention and shareholder rewards, dividend policy up to 30% of consolidated PAT with flexibility for lower payouts, strategic capital commitment areas (organic/inorganic growth, manufacturing, working capital, R&D), and dividend per share and payout ratio trends from FY 2019-20 to FY 2024-25, including a proposed dividend per share of ₹16 for FY 2024-25.

nodes.title: Capital allocation 9
nodes.summary: The text covers Cipla's R&D expenditure trends from FY 2019-20 to FY 2024-25, showing absolute spending and as a percentage of revenue, along with progress on product filings and priority assets. It references the ANDA/NDA portfolio and pipeline on page 74. Capital allocation strategy is detailed, including balancing cash retention for operations, growth, and contingencies with shareholder rewards. The dividend policy allows up to 30% of consolidated PAT, with flexibility for lower dividends. It lists capital uses: organic/inorganic growth, manufacturing infrastructure, working capital, and R&D. Dividend per share and payout ratio trends are provided from FY 2019-20 to FY 2024-25, with a proposed dividend of ₹16 per share for FY 2024-25.

nodes.title: Management Discussion and Analysis
nodes.summary: Cipla's Management Discussion and Analysis covers its 90-year healthcare commitment, business transformation, and focus on respiratory care, including investments in automation, digitalization, talent, quality, and R&D. It details global market trends (2014–2028), key therapy areas (oncology, immunology, diabetes, etc.), regulatory updates, advanced therapies, health tech, and AI. Financial highlights, One-India business performance (branded prescription, trade generics, consumer health), in-licensing deals, and FY 2025-26 outlook are included. Therapy sections cover market rankings, trade generics, consumer health, North America, One Africa (South Africa, Sub-Saharan Africa, North Africa, Global Access, Emerging Markets and Europe), and API business with financial results, launches, and strategic outlooks. It addresses opportunities from Double Materiality Assessment, threats (geopolitical instability, trade protectionism, etc.), Enterprise Risk Management, internal controls, and Internal Audit.

nodes.title: Management Discussion and Analysis (intro)
nodes.summary: Cipla's Management Discussion and Analysis covers its 90-year healthcare commitment, business transformation, and focus on respiratory care. It highlights investments in automation, digitalization, talent development, quality management, and R&D in respiratory, peptides, and biosimilars. The document details global market trends (2014–2028), including spending growth, key therapy areas (oncology, immunology, diabetes, cardiovascular, neurology), and Cipla's alignment in respiratory, oncology, and chronic therapies. It discusses regulatory updates (NLEM 2022), advanced therapies, health tech innovations, medical devices, and AI initiatives. Financial highlights, One-India business performance (branded prescription, trade generics, consumer health), in-licensing deals, and outlook for FY 2025-26 are also included.

nodes.title: Therapy
nodes.summary: The text covers Cipla's corporate overview and financial highlights, including market rankings and growth across therapies, in-licensing deals, and sales figures. It details the trade generics business transition and outlook, consumer health business performance with brand rankings and acquisition, North America's record revenue and product launches, and pipeline updates. It also covers the One Africa region's performance across South Africa (private and tender markets), Sub-Saharan Africa, North Africa, Cipla Global Access, and Emerging Markets and Europe, with financial results, market shares, therapy-wise performance, key launches, and strategic outlooks for FY 2025-26.

nodes.title: Therapy
nodes.summary: The text covers Cipla's API business, including therapy areas and geographies, FY 2025-26 outlook, manufacturing capabilities, business performance, and human resources. It details API experience, DMF filings, manufacturing sites, R&D centers, sustainability initiatives, and revenue by geography and therapy. It also discusses headwinds, revenue of USD 67 million, customer base, partnerships, and future priorities. Additionally, it mentions HR management and adherence to accounting standards.

nodes.title: Opportunities
nodes.summary: The text refers to page 48 for opportunities on material topics in the Double Materiality Assessment. It outlines threats like geopolitical instability, trade protectionism, anti-obesity medication popularity, government pricing, and market competition that can impact financial stability. Cipla's Enterprise Risk Management program covers key risks, with quarterly reviews by the Investment and Risk Management Committee. Page 54 provides the ERM framework and key risks with mitigation measures. The text also details internal controls: adequate systems commensurate with business nature, policies covering financial, operating, and compliance functions, providing reasonable assurance on operational effectiveness, fraud prevention, asset safeguarding, legal compliance, accurate accounting, and timely financial reporting. Internal Financial Controls align with the Companies Act, 2013 and COSO framework. The Internal Audit function reports to the Audit Committee, supported by internal teams and external firms.

nodes.title: Board’s Report
nodes.summary: The Board's Report covers the Company's audited financial statements for FY 2024-25, including standalone and consolidated financial summaries (revenue, profit, comprehensive income, surplus, dividend appropriations), share capital changes from ESOS/ESAR allotments, recommended final and special dividends, Management Discussion and Analysis, CSR initiatives, Integrated Annual Report, Business Responsibility & Sustainability Report, Corporate Governance report, Directors' Responsibility Statement, energy conservation and technology absorption disclosures, share-based incentive schemes, human resources and remuneration disclosures, loans/guarantees/investments, annual return, vigil mechanism, prevention of sexual harassment, related party transactions, internal financial controls, risk management, board evaluation, subsidiaries/associates/joint ventures (including changes), Nomination and Remuneration and Board Diversity Policy, directors and KMP changes, independent directors' declarations, board committees, statutory/secretarial/cost auditors and their reports, other regulatory disclosures, and acknowledgements.

nodes.title: Annual report on Corporate Social Responsibility (‘CSR’) activities pursuant to Rule 8 of the Companies (Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) Rules, 2014 as amended from time to time
nodes.summary: This annual CSR report covers the CSR policy's 'Caring for Life' philosophy, guiding principles, implementation modes, and key focus areas (health, education, skilling, environment, etc.). It details the CSR Committee's composition and meeting attendance, web-links for policy and projects, and an impact assessment summary using OECD DAC criteria, highlighting healthcare, education, skilling, environment, and disaster management outcomes. Financial disclosures include average net profit, CSR obligation, amounts spent on projects, administrative overheads, impact assessment, unspent amounts transferred to an unspent CSR account, and excess set-off. It also addresses unspent CSR amounts for preceding years, capital assets created, and confirms no failure to spend two percent of average net profit.

nodes.title: Secretarial Audit Report
key_items: For the financial year ended 31 st March, 2025
nodes.summary: This Secretarial Audit Report for Cipla Limited for FY 2024-25 covers compliance with statutory provisions including the Companies Act, SCRA, Depositories Act, FEMA, and SEBI regulations, noting no transactions requiring compliance with certain regulations like buy-back or delisting. It details board composition changes, including retirements, resignations, and appointments of directors and KMPs. Board processes are reviewed, including committee compliance, notice procedures, and unanimous decisions. Management responsibilities and compliance mechanisms are outlined, covering maintenance of secretarial records, filings, registers, meetings, remuneration, CSR spending, IEPF transfers, and employee stock schemes. The report confirms no fraud and no major events affecting the company, and includes an annexure reiterating management responsibilities and audit scope.

nodes.title: Annexure A to the Secretarial Audit Report for the financial year ended 31 st March, 2025
nodes.summary: This annexure to the Secretarial Audit Report for Cipla Limited for FY 2024-25 outlines the responsibilities of management and auditors. It states that management is responsible for secretarial records and legal compliance, while the auditor's role is to express an opinion on those records. The letter details the audit approach: following appropriate practices, considering independent legal opinions, verifying records on a test basis, and examining compliance procedures. It clarifies that financial records were not verified and that management representations were obtained. It includes a disclaimer that the report is not an assurance of future viability or management effectiveness. The document concludes with the auditor's signature, firm details, date, and place.

nodes.title: Cipla's Corporate Governance Philosophy and Pillars
key_items: Transparency; Fairness; Accountability; Competent leadership and management; Empowerment; Sustainability; Compliance and risk management
nodes.summary: This report outlines Cipla's corporate governance philosophy, rooted in compassion and care, with the purpose 'Caring for Life' guiding decisions. It emphasizes creating long-term shareholder value through ethical behavior and zero tolerance for deviations. The framework is built on pillars: transparency through accurate disclosures; fairness and integrity in transactions; accountability to all stakeholders via end-to-end ownership; competent leadership with a diverse and experienced board; empowerment of leaders and employees for high performance; sustainability managing financial, social, and environmental aspects; and compliance and risk management to mitigate risks and ensure corporate performance sustainability.

nodes.title: Governance structure

The Board's composition is diverse and compliant with regulations, with details on director categories, skills, and profiles. The section covers board membership criteria and selection process, the Board's role in strategic, operational, and financial matters, and governance items like risk management and performance evaluation. It details the annual board performance evaluation process and outcomes, actions taken on prior recommendations, board succession planning, meeting procedures, and independent directors' compliance, roles, meetings, and familiarisation/induction programs.

The Whistle Blower Policy/Vigil Mechanism applies globally to employees, board members, contractors, and others, detailing reporting, investigation, confidentiality, protection, and record retention. nodes.title: Key Accounting Judgments: Income Taxes, R&D Costs, Provisions
nodes.summary: The text addresses significant accounting judgments across three areas. Income taxes cover determining tax provisions, assessing probable tax positions, and evaluating deferred tax asset realisability based on future taxable income, reversals, and tax planning. Research and development costs are expensed as incurred unless capitalisation criteria for internally generated intangibles are met, typically after major-market regulatory approval; payments to third parties are expensed unless they transfer intellectual property, while in-licensing and acquisition payments are capitalised, with subsequent internal R&D expensed. Provisions and contingent liabilities involve judging whether matters are possible, probable, or remote, measuring exposures from litigation and claims, quantifying settlement ranges, and reviewing and reversing provisions at each balance sheet date.

It also summarizes estimates for: useful lives and residual values of property, plant, and equipment and intangible assets; refund liabilities for sales returns, including recognition of a return asset; provisions for rebates and discounts; inventory obsolescence; and expected credit losses under Ind AS 109 using the simplified approach and a provision matrix adjusted for forward-looking estimates.

nodes.title: Accounting Estimates: Useful Lives, Refund Liabilities, Rebates, Inventory Obsolescence
nodes.summary: The page covers accounting estimates: useful lives of property, plant and equipment and intangible assets, including determination and periodic review; refund liabilities for sales returns, including accrual, estimation factors, recognition of a return asset, and remeasurement; provisions for rebates and discounts, estimated based on historical averages and contract prices and recorded as revenue reduction; and inventories obsolescence, considering factors like shelf life, discontinuances, price changes, ageing, and competitive products, with periodic adjustments.

nodes.title: Expected credit loss
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies: Expected credit loss under Ind AS 109 using simplified approach for trade receivables, contract assets, lease receivables, and provision matrix; other assets assessed for significant credit risk increase with 12-month or lifetime ECL. Defined benefit plans accounting uses actuarial assumptions and estimates. Impairment of non-financial assets recognizes loss when carrying amount exceeds recoverable amount, based on estimated future cash flows and discount rate. Fair value of financial instruments uses valuation techniques with market inputs and estimates. Property, plant and equipment policy covers recognition at cost, depreciation (freehold land not depreciated), business combination treatment, subsequent costs, capital work-in-progress, and capital advances.

nodes.title: Accounting Policies: Credit Risk, Benefits, Impairment, Fair Value, PP&E
nodes.summary: The page covers several accounting topics: (vi) credit risk assessment for other assets, measuring 12-month or lifetime expected credit losses based on significant risk increase; (vii) accounting for defined benefit plans, including actuarial assumptions and factors like discount rates and mortality; (viii) impairment of non-financial assets, estimating recoverable amounts via future cash flows and discount rates; (viii) fair value of financial instruments, using valuation techniques with market inputs and estimates; and section 1.3 Material Accounting Policies, focusing on 1.3.1 Property, plant and equipment and Capital work-in-progress, covering recognition, measurement, depreciation, business combinations, subsequent costs, and capital advances.

nodes.title: 1.3.1 Property, plant and equipment and Capital work-inprogress (i) Recognition and measurement
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies from Cipla's standalone financial statements: impairment of financial assets using ECL based on credit risk; defined benefit plans using actuarial assumptions; non-financial asset impairment via future cash flow estimates and discount rates; fair value measurement of financial instruments using valuation techniques. It details property, plant and equipment recognition, measurement, capitalization of software and capital work-in-progress, depreciation methods and useful lives, and de-recognition. Intangible assets are covered, including recognition, in-process research and development, and regulatory approval expenditure.

nodes.title: Depreciation, De-recognition, and Intangible Assets Accounting Policies
key_items: In-Process Research and Development assets (“IPR&D”) or Intangible assets under development
nodes.summary: The page covers accounting policies for property, plant, and equipment and intangible assets. It details depreciation methods, useful lives, and review of residual values. It addresses capital work-in-progress, impairment review, and de-recognition of assets. For intangible assets, it covers recognition, measurement, and capitalisation of subsequent expenditures. It also explains treatment of In-Process Research and Development (IPR&D) assets, including non-amortisation, impairment evaluation, and capitalisation criteria for development expenditure.

The amortisation expense on intangible assets with finite life is recognised in standalone statement of profit and loss under the head depreciation, impairment and amortisation expense.

nodes.title: (v) De-recognition of intangible assets
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies: de-recognition of intangible assets (disposal or no future benefits, loss measurement), discontinued operations (criteria, presentation), assets held for sale (classification, measurement at lower of carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell, impairment recognition and reversal, no depreciation), investment properties (definition, initial measurement, subsequent expenditure capitalization, depreciation over 5-60 years), discontinued operations presentation, impairment of non-financial assets (annual testing for goodwill and indefinite-life intangibles, recoverable amount as higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use, cash-generating units, goodwill allocation, impairment loss recognition and allocation, reversal except goodwill, associate goodwill tested as part of investment), and foreign currency translation.

nodes.title: Foreign currency transactions and balances
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies: foreign currency transactions translated at transaction date rates, monetary items at reporting date rates, non-monetary items at historical or fair value rates. Inventories measured at lower of cost (weighted average) and net realizable value, including raw materials, packing materials, stores, spares, work-in-progress, stock-in-trade, and finished goods; cost includes acquisition, conversion, and overheads. Government grants recognized when assurance exists, as income over related costs or as deferred income over asset life; export entitlements recognized as other operating revenue when right is established. Revenue recognition covers sale of products (net of incentives, returns, rebates, taxes, discounts; variable consideration estimated), sales by clearing and forwarding agents, out-licensing arrangements (upfront fees, milestones, royalties), service fee, and profit sharing revenues.

nodes.title: Revenue Recognition Policies for Products, Agents, Licensing, and Services
key_items: Sales by clearing and forwarding agents
nodes.summary: The page outlines revenue recognition policies under section 1.3.9: (i) Sale of products—revenue recognized upon transfer of control, net of incentives, returns, rebates, taxes, and discounts, with variable consideration estimated using expected value or historical methods. (ii) Sales by clearing and forwarding agents—revenue recognized upon delivery to distributors, agents compensated on commission. (iii) Out-licensing arrangements—upfront payments, milestone payments, and royalties recognized based on delivery, performance obligations, and accrual basis, with variable consideration estimated. (iv) Service fee—revenue recognized as services are performed, with upfront non-refundable payments deferred over the service period.

nodes.title: Profit sharing revenues
nodes.summary: The text covers profit-sharing arrangements where Cipla sells products to business partners at a base price and earns additional profit share based on net sales or profits, recognizing base revenue upon delivery and profit share when highly probable. It details contract balances: contract assets for conditional earned consideration and contract liabilities for advance payments recognized as revenue upon performance. Other income sections explain recognition of interest income on a time basis using effective interest rate, dividend income when right to receive is established, and other income like rent and insurance claims when probable and measurable. Employee benefits include short-term benefits recognized undiscounted as services are rendered, defined contribution plans charged when contributions accrue, and defined benefit plans like provident fund managed by a trust with monthly contributions.

nodes.title: Revenue Recognition, Other Income, and Employee Benefit Accounting Policies
nodes.summary: The page covers accounting policies: revenue from business partners includes base sale price and profit share recognized when highly probable; contract assets and liabilities are defined and recognized based on timing of payment versus performance. Other income includes interest income accrued using effective interest rate, dividend income recognized when right to receive is established, and other income (rent, insurance claim, vendor settlement, miscellaneous) recognized when probable and measurable. Employee benefits include short-term benefits measured undiscounted and recognized when service rendered, and defined contribution plans (Employees’ Pension scheme, Labour Welfare Fund, ESIC) charged to profit and loss when contributions accrue, with no further obligation.

nodes.title: Defined benefit plans
nodes.summary: The text details employee benefit plans: defined benefit provident fund with joint contributions, government rate guarantees, and actuarial shortfall recognition; gratuity obligations using projected unit credit method, with re-measurements in other comprehensive income and net interest cost in profit or loss; other benefit plans including compensated absences (short-term undiscounted, long-term actuarial) and termination benefits recognized at specified dates; other long-term employee benefits discounted to present value; and equity-settled share-based payments recognized per Ind AS 102, with fair value expensed over vesting period and proceeds allocated to share capital and premium.

nodes.title: Employee Benefit Plans and Termination Benefits
nodes.summary: The text covers defined benefit obligations, including a provident fund plan where the Company must provide a government-declared minimum return, with contributions and interest shortfalls expensed. Gratuity obligations are valued using the projected unit credit method, with remeasurements in other comprehensive income and net interest cost in profit or loss. Other benefit plans address compensated absences: short-term liabilities are recognized undiscounted, while long-term liabilities are actuarially valued with gains/losses immediately expensed. Termination benefits are recognized when the Company can no longer withdraw the offer or when restructuring costs are recognized, with benefits due beyond 12 months discounted to present value.

nodes.title: (vi) Other long-term employee benefits
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for other long-term employee benefits (net obligation discounted to present value), share-based payments (equity-settled plans, fair value expensed over vesting period per Ind AS 102, exercise proceeds allocated to share capital and premium), taxes (current tax based on enacted rates with offsetting, deferred tax using balance sheet approach with recognition criteria and measurement at substantively enacted rates, and uncertain tax positions using most likely or expected value method), and leases (asset classes, contract assessment based on identified asset, economic benefits, and right to direct use).

nodes.title: Accounting Policy for Current and Deferred Income Taxes
nodes.summary: The page outlines the accounting policy for income taxes, covering current and deferred tax. It states income tax expense comprises current and deferred tax, recognized in profit or loss unless related to items in OCI or equity. Current tax is the payable on taxable income per applicable tax law, calculated using enacted rates, including prior-year adjustments, with offsetting criteria. Deferred tax uses the balance sheet approach on temporary differences. It details recognition of deferred tax assets based on probable taxable profit, exceptions for initial recognition, annual review and reduction of carrying amounts, reassessment of unrecognized assets, measurement using substantively enacted rates, recognition of liabilities for investments in subsidiaries and associates with specified exceptions, and offsetting criteria for deferred tax assets and liabilities.

nodes.title: (iii) Uncertain tax positions
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies: uncertain tax positions, including management judgments, measurement methods, and recognition criteria; leases, detailing asset classes, lease identification criteria, right-of-use asset and lease liability recognition, measurement, depreciation, remeasurement, and presentation; cash and cash equivalents definition; and provisions, covering recognition criteria, measurement at best estimate, discounting, and finance cost recognition.

nodes.title: Provision for onerous contracts
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for provisions for onerous contracts, contingent liabilities and assets, and financial instruments. It explains recognition and measurement of onerous contract provisions, disclosure of contingent liabilities and non-recognition of contingent assets. For financial instruments, it defines them and details initial recognition and measurement of financial assets, including trade receivables, subsequent measurement categories (amortised cost, FVTOCI, FVTPL, and equity instruments at FVTOCI), derecognition principles, and impairment using the expected credit loss model with a simplified approach for trade receivables.

nodes.title: (ii) Financial liabilities
nodes.summary: The text details accounting policies for financial liabilities: initial recognition and measurement (classification as FVTPL, loans/borrowings, payables, or hedging derivatives; initial fair value net of transaction costs); subsequent measurement (amortised cost using effective interest method or FVTPL); FVTPL classification (held for trading or designated; gains/losses in profit or loss, with own credit risk changes in OCI unless mismatch); amortised cost measurement (EIR method, interest expense in finance costs); and de-recognition (when obligation discharged, cancelled, or expires; replacement/modification treated as de-recognition of original and recognition of new liability, with difference in profit or loss).

nodes.title: (iii) Derivative financial instruments
nodes.summary: The text covers hedge accounting classifications: fair value hedges and cash flow hedges, detailing recognition, measurement, gains/losses treatment, and discontinuation criteria. It also addresses financial guarantee contracts, including initial and subsequent measurement and fair value determination, and offsetting financial instruments with criteria for net reporting. Finally, it outlines business combinations using the acquisition method, including control assessment, goodwill measurement, bargain purchase gains, contingent consideration, and step acquisitions.

nodes.title: Financial guarantee contracts
nodes.summary: The text covers hedge accounting and financial guarantee contracts. It explains that the ineffective portion of hedges is recognized immediately in profit and loss under other income/expenses, while the effective portion in equity is reclassified to profit and loss when the hedged item affects profit and loss. When a hedge expires, is sold, terminated, or fails criteria, cumulative deferred gains/losses remain in equity until the forecast transaction occurs; if the transaction is no longer expected, they are immediately reclassified to profit and loss. Financial guarantee contracts are recognized as liabilities at fair value initially, then at the higher of expected credit loss model amount or initially recognized amount less cumulative income. Fair value is based on present value of cash flow differences or estimated third-party payment. Guarantees for associates provided without compensation are treated as contributions to investment cost.

nodes.title: Offsetting financial instruments
nodes.summary: The text covers offsetting financial instruments with legal enforceability and intention for net settlement. It details business combinations using the acquisition method, including identifying a business, the concentration test, control assessment, goodwill measurement, bargain purchase gains, consideration transferred, contingent consideration, contingent liabilities, non-controlling interests, transaction costs, common control transactions, and provisional accounting. It also covers exceptional items disclosure, recent accounting pronouncements (Ind AS 117 and amendments to Ind AS 116) with no significant impact, and note that no new standards are issued but not yet effective. Finally, it presents a property, plant and equipment note with gross carrying values, additions, transfers, deletions, accumulated depreciation and impairment, net carrying values, and footnotes on research and development additions, impairment charges, title deeds, no revaluation, and no charges created.

nodes.title: A. Accounting classification and fair value measurement; The following methods and assumptions were used to estimate the fair values:
key_items: A. Accounting classification and fair value measurement
The following methods and assumptions were used to estimate the fair values:
nodes.summary:
Note 45: Financial instruments
A. Accounting classification and fair value measurement
The fair value of financial assets and liabilities are included at the amount at which the instrument could be exchanged in a current transaction between willing parties, other than in a forced or liquidation sale.
The following methods and assumptions were used to estimate the fair values:
The carrying amount of trade receivable, lease liability, trade payable, loans, cash and cash equivalents, other bank balances and other receivables as at 31st March, 2025 and 31st March, 2024 are considered to be the same as their fair values, due to their short-term nature.
Financial Instruments with fixed and variable interest rates are evaluated by the company based on parameters such as interest rate and individual credit worthiness of the counterparty. Based on this evaluation, allowances are taken to account for the expected losses of these receivables.

nodes.title: Fair value hierarchy
nodes.summary: The text details the fair value hierarchy (Levels 1-3) with definitions and examples, presents tables of carrying and fair values of financial instruments by category as of March 31, 2025 and 2024 (including assets and liabilities such as investments, loans, derivatives, and trade payables), notes no transfers between Level 1 and 2, provides a reconciliation of Level 3 fair values from opening to closing balances, and lists valuation techniques and significant unobservable inputs for Level 2 and Level 3 instruments such as deferred consideration, unquoted investments, and derivatives.

nodes.title: B. Financial risk management objectives and policies
nodes.summary: The text outlines the Company's financial risk management objectives and policies, covering exposure to market, credit, and liquidity risks, and the goal of minimizing adverse effects on financial performance. It lists financial liabilities (trade payables, other liabilities) and assets (trade receivables, security deposits, loans and advances). It describes the Risk Management Committee, a robust Business Risk Management framework for identifying and evaluating risks and opportunities, and periodic review by the Audit Committee. It then defines market risk and specifies the Company's exposure to currency risk, other price risk, and interest rate risk, noting these may affect income, expenses, or financial instrument values.

nodes.title: Market risk
nodes.summary: The text covers Note 45 on financial instruments from Cipla's 2024-25 standalone financial statements. It states no transfers between Level 1 and Level 2 fair values for both years, provides a reconciliation of Level 3 fair values from April 1, 2023 to March 31, 2025 for equity securities, deferred consideration, and other investments, and details valuation techniques and significant unobservable inputs for Level 2 and Level 3 instruments. It then outlines financial risk management objectives, including the Company's exposure to market, credit, and liquidity risks, the composition of financial liabilities and assets, the role of the Risk Management Committee, the Business Risk Management framework, Audit Committee oversight, and an introduction to market risk (currency, other price, and interest rate risks).

nodes.title: (a) Currency risk:
nodes.summary: The text discusses currency risk, noting the Company's international operations and exposure to foreign exchange risk due to mismatches in currencies for sales, services, and purchases. It mentions the use of derivative instruments like forward and option contracts to mitigate exchange rate risks. The volatility of the Indian Rupee against currencies such as USD, EUR, GBP, and ZAR is highlighted, affecting operations. It also includes a section on foreign exchange derivatives and exposures outstanding at year-end, with a table showing forward contracts sold, currency swaps, and options contracts as of March 31, 2024, and March 31, 2025, in crores.

nodes.title: Unhedged foreign exchange exposures:
nodes.summary: The text covers financial risk management disclosures: unhedged foreign exchange exposures by currency (USD, ZAR, AUD, INR) for receivables, cash, and payables; foreign currency risk from financial instruments as of March 31, 2025 and 2024 with amounts in USD, EUR, GBP, ZAR, and other currencies; sensitivity analysis showing 5% INR strengthening/weakening impact on profit or loss for each currency; other price risk from mutual fund investments (₹6,849.31 crore in 2025, ₹4,383.59 crore in 2024) with 1% price change sensitivity on profit/loss and OCI, plus equity investments measured at FVOCI; interest rate risk noting no borrowings and limited exposure; and credit risk with maximum exposure of ₹16,089.78 crore (2025) and ₹14,923.76 crore (2024), including receivables credit risk management.

nodes.title: Financial Instruments Sensitivity Analysis: Exchange and Price Risks
key_items: Movement in exchange rate (Strengthening of INR)
nodes.summary: This page presents sensitivity analyses for financial instruments as of March 31, 2025 and 2024. It details the impact of a 5% strengthening or weakening of the Indian rupee against foreign currencies (USD, EUR, GBP, ZAR, and others) on profit/loss and equity. It also covers other price risk, primarily from mutual fund investments, showing the effect of a 1% price change on profit/loss and other comprehensive income, along with the value of equity investments measured at fair value through OCI.

nodes.title: (c) Interest rate risk
nodes.summary: The text covers financial risk management, focusing on interest rate risk and credit risk. Interest rate risk includes fair value and cash flow risks; the Company has no borrowings but invests in debt mutual funds, with insignificant exposure due to short tenure. Credit risk arises from receivables and investments, with maximum exposure of H 16,089.78 Crores (2025) and H 14,923.76 Crores (2024). It details trade receivables management, high-rated cash equivalents, expected credit loss model under Ind AS 109, and changes in allowance for credit losses. Liquidity risk management is also discussed, including maintaining sufficient funds, cautious strategy, and contractual maturities of financial liabilities.

nodes.summary: This note details the Company's CSR compliance under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, including the formation of a CSR Committee, mandatory spending of at least 2% of average net profit, and focus areas such as health, education, skilling, environmental sustainability, disaster response, rural development, and R&D. It provides financial data in crores for FY 2025 and 2024: amount required to be spent (80.06 and 69.61), expenditure on asset construction/acquisition (5.53 and 8.40), other expenditure/unspent amounts deposited (74.54 and 67.48), shortfall (nil), related party transactions (0.68 and 0.69), and balance carried forward with opening, addition, utilization, and closing balances. It notes contributions to Cipla Foundation, surplus from CSR projects, set-off of excess spent, and an ongoing project with funds in a special account.

nodes.title: Note 47: Capital management A. Risk Management
nodes.summary: The text covers capital management, detailing objectives to safeguard going concern status, provide shareholder returns, and maintain optimal capital structure. It describes adjusting capital through dividends, share issuance, or asset sales, and monitors capital via a gearing ratio (net debt/equity) with net debt defined as total borrowings less cash, investments, and deposits. It provides comparative gearing ratio data for March 31, 2025 and 2024, showing net debt, total equity, and ratios. Additionally, it covers dividend on equity shares, including dividends paid during the year (final dividends for FY 2023-24 and FY 2022-23), proposed dividends not recognized as liability, and a Board-recommended final and special dividend subject to AGM approval.

nodes.title: Note 48: Earnings Per Share (EPS)
nodes.summary: Note 48 details Earnings Per Share (EPS) calculations, including basic EPS (net profit attributable to equity shareholders divided by weighted average equity shares) and diluted EPS (adjusted for dilutive potential equity shares like employee stock options, deemed converted at period start). It references Ind AS 33 disclosure requirements and presents comparative figures for years ended March 31, 2025 and 2024, covering profit from continuing and discontinuing/restructuring operations, basic and diluted weighted average shares, and basic and diluted EPS from continuing operations, discontinuing/restructuring operations, and total EPS, all with par value of ₹2 per share.

The note includes footnotes indicating that the principal business of the entities is pharmaceutical business, except two associates involved in renewable power generation.

nodes.title: Other Matter

It notes that 30 subsidiaries with total assets of ₹11,770.79 crores, revenues of ₹4,271.35 crores, and net cash inflows of ₹55.46 crores were not audited by the principal auditor; their financials were audited by other auditors. The auditor's opinion is based solely on other auditors' reports and management-certified information, and is not modified in respect of these matters.

nodes.title: Group Information
nodes.summary: Cipla Limited, an Indian public company with a registered office in Mumbai, manufactures, develops, and markets branded and generic formulations and APIs. It has manufacturing, trading, and incidental operations in India and internationally. Its equity shares are listed on the Bombay Stock Exchange and National Stock Exchange of India, and Global Depository Receipts on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange. The consolidated financial statements include Cipla Limited, its subsidiaries, and associates, collectively referred to as the Group.

nodes.title: Note 1: Basis of Preparation, Measurement, Key accounting estimates and judgements and Material accounting policies information

It details material accounting policies for income taxes, R&D costs, provisions, business combinations, refund liabilities, chargebacks and rebates, inventory obsolescence, expected credit losses, defined benefit plans, impairment of non-financial assets, fair value of financial instruments, property plant and equipment, intangible assets, investment properties, discontinued operations, foreign currency translation, inventories, government grants, revenue recognition (including product sales, licensing, services, and profit-sharing), contract balances, employee benefits (short-term, defined contribution, defined benefit, compensated absences, termination), share-based payments, leases, financial instruments (classification, measurement, de-recognition, impairment, derivatives, hedge accounting, guarantees, put options, offsetting), and contingent liabilities. It also lists subsidiaries, associates, and other consolidating entities, and provides details on property, plant and equipment, capital work-in-progress, and right-of-use assets.

nodes.title: Basis of Preparation, Measurement, and Material Accounting Policies

nodes.title: Investment in subsidiaries
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting for investments in subsidiaries, including the definition of control and consolidation from acquisition to disposal. It details recognition of goodwill (excess cost over equity share) and capital reserve (excess equity share over cost), with goodwill tested for impairment. Non-controlling interests (NCI) are defined, presented separately in equity, and valued at proportionate net assets at acquisition plus their share of subsequent equity movements. Consolidation is line-by-line with elimination of intra-group balances, transactions, and unrealized profits (and losses unless cost cannot be recovered). Transactions with NCI not losing control are treated as equity transactions, adjusting carrying amounts with differences recognized in equity. NCI share of profit and OCI is shown separately. On loss of control, assets, liabilities, NCI, and related equity components are derecognized, any gain/loss recognized in profit or loss, and retained interest measured at fair value and accounted for as equity-accounted investee or financial asset (FVTOCI or FVTPL).

nodes.title: Investment in Associates
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting for investments in associates using the equity method, including initial recognition at cost, adjustments for profit or loss, policy alignments, elimination of unrealised gains/losses, impairment testing of underlying assets, and cessation/resumption of loss recognition. It also addresses key accounting estimates and judgements, emphasizing management's prudent estimates reviewed at each reporting date with prospective recognition of revisions. Critical judgements include lease term determination under Ind AS 116, considering options to extend/terminate, leasehold improvements, termination costs, asset importance, location, and alternatives, with reassessment in future periods.

nodes.title: (ii) Income taxes
nodes.summary: The text covers income taxes for the Group, highlighting major tax jurisdictions in India, US, and South Africa, with filings in other foreign jurisdictions. It discusses significant judgments in determining income tax provisions, including whether tax positions are probable of being sustained, and the complexity of tax assessments resolved over extended periods. It notes management's individual assessment of taxes subject to legal or economic limits or uncertainties. Additionally, it addresses assessing the realisability of deferred tax assets, considering future taxable income, scheduled reversals of deferred tax liabilities, projected income, and tax planning strategies. Management believes the Group will realise benefits based on historical and projected income, though realisable amounts could be reduced if future income estimates decline.

nodes.title: (iii) Research and development costs
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for R&D costs, provisions and contingent liabilities, business combinations, and key estimates. R&D expenses are generally expensed unless related to acquired intellectual property or when regulatory approval is obtained. Provisions and contingent liabilities require judgment in assessing likelihood and measurement, with regular review. Business combinations use the acquisition method, with judgment in determining control and acquisition date. Estimates include useful lives of property, plant, equipment, and intangibles, refund liabilities for expected sales returns with corresponding assets, and provisions for chargebacks, rebates, and discounts based on historical data.

nodes.title: Accounting Judgements: Provisions, Business Combinations, and Refund Liabilities
nodes.summary: The text addresses key accounting judgements and estimates. It covers provisions and contingent liabilities, including assessing likelihood, measuring exposures, and reviewing provisions. Business combinations are accounted for using the acquisition method, with judgement applied to determine acquisition date, control, and whether it is a business or asset acquisition. It also discusses estimates of useful lives and residual values for property, plant and equipment and intangible assets. Refund liabilities are recognized for expected sales returns based on historical experience, market factors, and product characteristics, with a corresponding asset for returned goods measured at former carrying amount less recovery costs, and both are remeasured periodically.

nodes.title: Provision for chargeback, rebates and discounts
nodes.summary: The text details accounting provisions: chargebacks, rebates, and discounts are estimated and recorded as revenue reductions based on historical rates, contract prices, and inventory levels; shelf stock adjustments are credits for price decreases due to competition, based on contract terms; inventory obsolescence provisions consider shelf life, discontinuances, price changes, ageing, and new products; expected credit loss under Ind AS 109 uses a simplified approach with a provision matrix for trade receivables and assesses significant credit risk increases for other assets; defined benefit plans rely on actuarial assumptions like discount rates, compensation increases, and turnover; and impairment of non-financial assets compares carrying amount to recoverable amount using estimated future cash flows and suitable discount rates.

nodes.title: Key Accounting Policies: Inventory Adjustments, Credit Loss, and Benefit Plans
nodes.summary: This page outlines four accounting policies: shelf stock adjustments, which are credits for price declines due to competition; inventories obsolescence, detailing factors for provisioning slow-moving or obsolete stock; expected credit loss, explaining the simplified approach under Ind AS 109 for trade receivables using a provision matrix and forward-looking estimates, and the general approach for other assets; and accounting for defined benefit plans, covering actuarial assumptions like discount rates, compensation increases, and demographic estimates subject to significant judgement.

nodes.title: (viii) Impairment of non-financial assets
nodes.summary:
(viii) Impairment of non-financial assets
An impairment loss is recognised for the amount by which an asset’s or cash-generating unit’s carrying amount exceeds its recoverable amount. To determine the recoverable amount, management estimates expected future cash flows from each asset or cash-generating unit and determines a suitable interest rate in order to calculate the present value of those cash flows. In the process of measuring expected future cash flows, management makes assumptions about future operating results. These assumptions relate to future events and circumstances. The actual results may vary and may cause significant adjustments to the Group’s assets.
In most cases, determining the applicable discount rate involves estimating the appropriate adjustment to market risk and the appropriate adjustment to asset-specific risk factors.
